action.description: Action object MUST contain a field `submission`, and MAY contain arbitrary additional information.

actTimeout.description: Maximum runtime (seconds) to obtain an action from an agent.

episodeSteps.description: Maximum number of steps in the episode.

includeLegalActions.description: If true, include legalActions and legalActionStrings in observations. Defaults to false since these can be derived from serializedGameAndState.

initialActions.description: Actions applied to initial state before play begins to set up starting position.

loadPresetHands.description: Repeated poker only. Load preset hand chance actions from preset_hands.jsonl.

openSpielGameName.description: The short_name of the OpenSpiel game to load.

openSpielGameParameters.description: Game parameters for Open Spiel game.

openSpielGameString.description: The full game string including parameters.

presetHands.description: Repeated poker only. List of per-hand chance action sequences to use instead of random chance.

runTimeout.description: Maximum runtime (seconds) of an episode (not necessarily DONE).

savePrompt.description: If true, the LLM prompt produced by the harness is included as a 'prompt' field on the action returned by core_harness, which causes it to be persisted in the episode replay. Defaults to false to keep replays small.

seed.description: Integer currently only used for selecting starting position.

strictMode.description: If true, agents must return only {'submission': int} (no extra fields like 'thoughts'), and per-agent TIMEOUT/ERROR/INVALID counts as a loss for the offending agent only — other agents win. If false (default), any agent error halts and voids the entire episode, matching the lenient research-mode behavior.

useImage.description: If true, indicates the observation is intended to be rendered as an image. Note that currently the agent harness is responsible for the actual rendering; no image is passed in the observation.

useOpenings.description: Whether to start from a position in an opening book.

currentPlayer.description: ID of player whose turn it is.

legalActionStrings.description: List of OpenSpiel legal action strings. Only included if includeLegalActions is true.

legalActions.description: List of OpenSpiel legal action integers. Only included if includeLegalActions is true.

openSpielGameName.description: Short name of the OpenSpiel game.

playerId.description: ID of the agent receiving this observation.

serializedGameAndState.description: Enables reconstructing the Game and State objects.

remainingOverageTime.description: Total remaining banked time (seconds) that can be used in excess of per-step actTimeouts -- agent is disqualified with TIMEOUT status when this drops below 0.

action.thoughts:
The current board position shows only two pieces played so far: an x at the very bottom of the central column (row 5, column 3) and an o directly above it (row 4, column 3). All other cells are empty, and it is x's turn to move. With so few pieces on the board, no immediate win or forced threat exists for either player, so the focus must be on building connected groups of x pieces while contesting the center and limiting o's options.

Playing in column 3 would drop an x to row 3 in that column. This creates an x-o-x stack vertically. While it occupies central space, the two x pieces remain disconnected (with o blocking any vertical line through column 3), and the original bottom x is left isolated. This does not build any immediate line or double threat and allows o to potentially respond elsewhere to start their own connected group.

A stronger approach is to play adjacent to the existing x piece to create a connected pair. Dropping in column 2 places a new x at row 5, column 2. This immediately connects horizontally with the x at row 5, column 3, forming the start of a bottom-row line. From here, x can later extend left (column 1) or build diagonals upward (e.g., toward row 4/column 1 or row 3/column 0). Column 2 is central enough to maintain balance while creating flexible attacking options. (Column 4 is fully symmetric and equally viable, but column 2 works equivalently.)

This move forces o to respond (potentially by blocking the new pair or contesting the center themselves), while preserving x's initiative in the center-left area. All other columns (0, 1, 5, 6) are too far from the existing pieces and cede too much central control.

Final Answer: 2

action.thoughts:
The current board has only four pieces placed: my x's in columns 2 and 3 of the bottom row (row 5), plus opponent's o's in column 4 of row 5 and column 3 of row 4. This is an early-game position with no completed lines of three or more for either player.

My two adjacent x pieces in the bottom row allow for an immediate forcing move. Dropping an x into column 1 places it at row 5, column 1. This creates three consecutive x pieces horizontally across row 5, columns 1-3. The only open extension to complete four-in-a-row is column 0 (column 4 is blocked by the opponent's o). This creates an immediate threat: on my next turn I can win by playing in column 0 unless the opponent blocks it first.

No other legal column creates an equivalent immediate threat:
- Playing in column 2, 3, 4, or 5 adds a piece but results in at most two connected pieces (no line of three).
- Playing in column 0 or 6 leaves disconnected pieces with no line of three.
- Playing in column 3 or 4 also fails to align with my existing x pieces into a line of three.

The opponent has a potential future diagonal line (columns 2-4) but cannot complete it on their immediate turn. By creating a win threat now, I force the opponent to respond defensively in column 0 on their turn. This seizes the initiative and allows me to build additional threats (e.g., diagonal setups or new horizontal/vertical lines) on my subsequent turn while the opponent is occupied blocking.

This is the optimal move per standard Connect Four strategy: prioritize creating forcing threats over passive development when the board is open.

Final Answer: 1
